title: Reporting suspicious mail: who to tell, and how
body_md:
## Tell the right people, and don’t pass it round

A parcel nobody ordered is sitting in the lobby, and the label looks official. Nobody opens it, and nobody carries it around the office to show everyone. You call whoever deals with these things, and you say honestly whether you touched it. A suspicious email deserves the same handling.

Spotting it is useful, and getting it in front of people who can review it may protect others too. A report is **not** a guarantee that a campaign will be blocked, that money will be recovered, or that every copy will vanish. Treat it as one calm step. What comes after depends on what you actually exposed: if your accounts or payments were touched, deal with those too.

### Pick the right address

For personal mail, use your provider’s built-in phishing report where there is one. In Gmail on a computer, open the menu beside Reply and choose **Report phishing**. Google says a message you report by hand, attachments included, may be copied and analyzed to protect against abuse. Outlook.com has **Report → Report phishing**, and Microsoft notes that reporting a sender does not by itself stop that sender’s future messages. Menu names and positions change from time to time.

For work or school mail, use your organization’s report button, or the channel named in its policy. Keep the message until the team tells you what to do with it; some want the original attached so the headers survive. Don’t send a live suspicious email to a long list of colleagues. A screenshot can help a discussion, but the security team may need the original to analyze.

In the UK, the NCSC asks people to forward doubtful emails to report@phishing.gov.uk. In the US, the FTC points to ReportFraud.ftc.gov and, for phishing email, to the Anti-Phishing Working Group. These are local options, not one worldwide mailbox. Check the official, current instructions before you send, especially if the message holds private workplace or customer information.

### Then deal with what happened

Don’t reply to a message you think is malicious, don’t open its attachment, and don’t use its unsubscribe link. A subscription you chose yourself is a different matter: use the provider’s normal unsubscribe control or your account settings. After you report, follow your provider’s or organization’s instructions on moving the message to Junk, keeping it or deleting it; there is no universal “leave it in quarantine” rule. If you clicked, downloaded a file, entered credentials or paid, tell support what happened and start the right recovery steps promptly, through channels you found yourself. Don’t hide a mistake out of embarrassment.

What you are after is an accurate signal, sent to the right place, with as little extra exposure as possible. “I’m not sure” is a perfectly good thing to write in a report. Suspicion is enough to ask for a second look.

widget_config.goal: Get a suspicious email to your provider or organization, and describe honestly what you did with it.
widget_config.today_action: Find the phishing-report control, or the security contact, for one mailbox you use. Note the route and send nothing for this exercise.
widget_config.scope: Gmail and Outlook steps describe those products as checked on 20 October 2026. The UK NCSC and US FTC routes apply only in those countries. Workplace policy and privacy rules come first.

blocks.title: A schedule nobody announced
blocks.situation: A message to several employees says a new work schedule is attached. The sender’s name looks like HR’s, but nobody announced a new schedule and the file is a surprise. A colleague asks you to forward it to them.
blocks.analysis: Don’t open the file, and don’t forward it, even to the colleague who asked. Use your workplace’s report channel and describe the claimed sender, the attachment and who received it. Ask HR through the staff directory whether it sent a schedule. Leave retention and containment to the security team.

blocks.title: The newsletter in Junk
blocks.situation: A newsletter you subscribed to has landed in Junk since the sender changed platforms. The topic and the sender’s name are familiar, but the address it arrives from has changed.
blocks.analysis: A changed address can be perfectly legitimate. Check your subscription in your account with the publisher or on its official site. If it checks out, use your mail app’s “not spam” control, and don’t report it as phishing just because a filter put it in Junk. If it ever asks for a password or a payment you didn’t expect, verify that separately.

blocks.title: The alert in the team mailbox
blocks.setup: An invented exercise. A team mailbox receives what claims to be a file-sharing alert. No real message or attachment is involved.

steps.prompt: The alert tells everyone to open an attachment. You haven’t touched it. What first?

choices.text: Leave the attachment closed and use the team’s report channel.
choices.consequence: Security gets the original by the route it expects.
choices.explanation: You can report without opening the file.

choices.text: Forward the whole message to your teammates as a warning.
choices.consequence: A working attachment lands in more inboxes.
choices.explanation: A wide forward spreads the very thing you are warning about.

steps.prompt: The report form asks whether anyone clicked on anything. You opened the message but never the file. What do you write?

choices.text: That you read the message and did not open the attachment, exactly as it happened.
choices.consequence: Responders can judge how much was really exposed.
choices.explanation: Plain facts help more than a confident guess.

choices.consequence: Responders get an inaccurate account of the incident.
choices.explanation: Reading a message is different from opening its link or file, and the report should say which one happened.

steps.prompt: A coworker says they opened the attachment and typed their password into the page it showed. What do you advise?

choices.text: Wait until security proves there has been a compromise.
choices.consequence: Recovery is held up while the account is at risk.
choices.explanation: A password that may have been exposed needs quick action.

choices.text: Contact security, and change the password in the real service, following their guidance.
choices.consequence: The exposure and the response reach the right team.
choices.explanation: If a code or an approval was involved, put that in the report too.

steps.prompt: Security later confirms it received a report about this message. What do you do with your own copy?

choices.text: Assume everyone is protected and delete it, whatever the policy says.
choices.consequence: You may throw away material the team needs.
choices.explanation: Filing a report does not mean every inbox is protected at once.

choices.text: Do what the team tells you: keep it, move it or delete it.
choices.consequence: The message and the mailbox are handled under local procedure.
choices.explanation: How long to keep it depends on the organization.

blocks.debrief: A good report is precise and goes to the right place. It does not replace recovery after exposure, and it does not switch on protection by itself. Retry the choices that spread the message or hid a detail.

questions.prompt: Your workplace has a dedicated phishing-report button, and a suspicious attachment arrives. What is best?

choices.text: Press the button, without opening the attachment or forwarding it around.
choices.explanation: Your security process receives the message.

choices.text: Forward it to every colleague and let them decide.

questions.prompt: A newsletter you asked for lands in Junk. Does that prove it is phishing?

choices.text: Yes; whatever the Junk folder decides is final.
No. Check the subscription separately, and mark it as not spam if it is genuine.
choices.explanation: A confusing but legitimate case needs checking, not an automatic accusation.

questions.prompt: You reported a suspicious sender in Outlook.com. What can you safely assume?

choices.text: The report went through, but the sender is not necessarily blocked.
choices.explanation: Microsoft says plainly that reporting and blocking are separate.

choices.text: Every future email from that sender is now blocked for everyone.
choices.explanation: A report does not promise that.

questions.prompt: You entered a password after following a suspected phishing link. Is reporting the email enough?

choices.text: Yes; a report restores the account automatically.
choices.explanation: Reporting and account recovery are separate things.

choices.text: No. Report what happened, change the password through the real service, and ask for support.
choices.explanation: Respond promptly to what was actually exposed.
